titles.Source section / Nephron wedge: One nephron and its collecting duct

Gross / major calyx.description: The major calyces are the two or three large cup-shaped branches of the collecting system. Each one forms by joining several minor calyces, and they drain into the renal pelvis.
clinical: Staghorn stone
A large branching stone can fill the renal pelvis and extend into the major and minor calyces. These stones are often linked to recurrent urinary infection.

Gross / minor calyx.description: The minor calyces are the small cup-shaped tubes that each fit over the tip of a renal papilla. They collect urine as it drips out of the papilla.

Gross / renal pelvis.description: The renal pelvis is the funnel-shaped chamber that collects urine from the major calyces. It narrows at the pelviureteric junction to become the ureter.
clinical: Hydronephrosis
A blockage below the pelvis, such as a stone or stricture at the pelviureteric junction, makes urine back up and swell the pelvis and calyces.
Pyelonephritis
Bacteria that climb up from the bladder infect the renal pelvis and then the kidney tissue, causing fever and flank pain.

Gross / ureter.description: The ureter is a muscular tube about 25 to 30 cm long that carries urine from the renal pelvis to the bladder. It runs down behind the peritoneum, lying on the psoas muscle.
clinical: Ureteric stones

Stones often lodge at three narrow points: where the ureter leaves the pelvis, where it crosses the pelvic brim, and where it enters the bladder. A stone there typically causes severe colicky flank pain.

Gross / abdominal aorta.description: The abdominal aorta is the main artery of the trunk below the diaphragm. It gives off the renal arteries, which supply the kidneys.

Gross / inferior vena cava.description: The inferior vena cava is the large vein that returns blood from the lower body to the right atrium. It receives both renal veins and runs on the right side of the aorta.

Gross / renal capsule.description: The renal capsule is a thin, tough layer of dense connective tissue wrapping the kidney directly. In a healthy kidney it strips off easily.

Gross / renal column.description: Renal columns are extensions of cortex that dip down between neighbouring pyramids toward the sinus. The interlobar arteries and veins run inside them.
clinical: Column that looks like a mass
An unusually large renal column can look like a tumour on ultrasound or CT, but it is normal tissue.

Gross / renal cortex.description: The renal cortex is the outer, granular layer of the kidney, between the capsule and the bases of the pyramids. It contains all the glomeruli and the convoluted parts of the tubules.

Gross / renal papilla.description: The renal papillae are the rounded tips of the pyramids, projecting into the minor calyces. Urine drips out through small openings in each papilla called the papillary ducts.
clinical: Papillary necrosis
The papillae can die when their blood supply is lost, as in long-term diabetes, urinary obstruction, or heavy use of analgesics such as NSAIDs. It can cause flank pain and blood in the urine.

Gross / renal pyramid.description: The renal pyramids are the cone-shaped masses of medulla, usually 8 to 18 per kidney. Their bases face the cortex and their tips form the papillae.

Gross / renal sinus fat.description: The renal sinus is the central space of the kidney that opens at the hilum and holds the pelvis, calyces and vessels. It is packed with fat that continues from the perirenal fat outside the kidney.

Gross / arcuate artery.description: Arcuate arteries arch over the bases of the pyramids at the boundary between cortex and medulla. They are end arteries that do not join each other, and they give off the interlobular arteries.

Gross / interlobar artery.description: Interlobar arteries run outward from the sinus beside the pyramids, through the renal columns, to reach the boundary between cortex and medulla. There they branch into the arcuate arteries.

Gross / interlobular artery.description: Interlobular arteries run out through the cortex from the arcuate arteries. They give off the afferent arterioles that feed each glomerulus.

Gross / renal artery.description: The renal artery branches from the side of the abdominal aorta and carries about a fifth to a quarter of the cardiac output to the kidneys. It divides at the hilum into anterior and posterior divisions.
clinical: Renovascular hypertension
Narrowing of the renal artery, usually from atherosclerosis, lowers kidney blood flow and triggers renin release, which raises blood pressure.

Gross / segmental artery.description: Segmental arteries are five branches in the renal sinus, each supplying one segment of the kidney. They are end arteries with no connections to their neighbours.
clinical: Renal infarction
A clot blocking a segmental artery causes a wedge-shaped infarct in that kidney segment, often with flank pain and blood in the urine.

Gross / arcuate vein.description: Arcuate veins arch over the pyramid bases alongside the arcuate arteries. Unlike the arteries, they join each other to form arches, and they collect blood from the interlobular veins.

Gross / interlobar vein.description: Interlobar veins run beside the interlobar arteries through the renal columns. They collect blood from the arcuate veins and carry it toward the renal sinus.

Gross / interlobular vein.description: Interlobular veins run through the cortex to the arcuate veins. They collect blood from the capillaries around the tubules.

Gross / gonadal vein.description: The left gonadal vein drains the testis or ovary on its side and joins the left renal vein. On the right, the gonadal vein drains directly into the inferior vena cava.

Gross / renal vein.description: The renal vein leaves the hilum in front of the renal artery and drains the kidney into the inferior vena cava. The left renal vein is longer, because it passes in front of the aorta.
clinical: Nutcracker phenomenon
The left renal vein can be squeezed between the aorta and the superior mesenteric artery, causing blood in the urine and flank pain.

Gross / renal vein trunk.description: These are the large veins inside the sinus that join together to form the renal vein at the hilum. Each trunk drains one region of the kidney, upper, middle or lower, and the upper and middle parts can share a common trunk before joining.

Nephron / Afferent arteriole endothelium.description: The afferent arteriole carries blood into each glomerulus, and its endothelium is the thin inner lining of that vessel. It is continuous with the lining of the rest of the arterial system.

Nephron / Afferent arteriole smooth musc.description: Smooth muscle in the wall of the afferent arteriole controls how much blood enters the glomerulus. Constricting it lowers the glomerular filtration rate.
clinical: NSAIDs and the kidney
NSAIDs block the prostaglandins that dilate the afferent arteriole, so they can reduce filtration, especially in people who are dehydrated or have heart failure.

Nephron / Efferent arteriole endothelium.description: The efferent arteriole carries blood away from the glomerulus, and it is narrower than the afferent arteriole. Its endothelium is a thin inner lining.

Nephron / Efferent arteriole smooth musc.description: Smooth muscle in the efferent arteriole can constrict to raise pressure inside the glomerulus. This helps keep filtration going when blood flow into the glomerulus falls.
clinical: ACE inhibitors and ARBs
These drugs stop angiotensin II from constricting the efferent arteriole, which lowers glomerular pressure and can reduce filtration.

Nephron / Extraglomerular mesangium (lac.description: Lacis cells sit in the angle between the afferent and efferent arterioles, beside the macula densa. They help link the sensing of salt at the macula densa to the arteriolar and renin-releasing cells.

Nephron / Juxtaglomerular (granular) cel.description: Juxtaglomerular cells are modified smooth muscle cells in the wall of the afferent arteriole. They release renin when blood pressure or salt delivery to the macula densa falls.
clinical: Renin and ACE inhibitors

ACE inhibitors block the conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II, which comes after renin acts. In bilateral renal artery stenosis they can cause acute kidney injury, because the kidney then depends on angiotensin II to keep glomerular pressure up.

Nephron / Macula densa.description: The macula densa is a small patch of specialized cells in the early distal tubule that touches the glomerulus. It senses the sodium chloride content of the filtrate and signals the nearby arteriole to adjust blood flow.

Nephron / Ascending vasa recta.description: Ascending vasa recta are thin capillary-like vessels that carry blood back up toward the cortex. They run alongside the loops of Henle and exchange salt and water with them.

Nephron / Cortical venule.description: The cortical venule is a small vein in the outer kidney that drains blood from the cortical capillaries into the larger veins.

Nephron / Descending vasa recta.description: Descending vasa recta carry blood down into the medulla alongside the loops of Henle. Their hairpin shape lets them supply the medulla without washing away its salt gradient.

Nephron / Peritubular capillaries.description: Peritubular capillaries wrap around the proximal and distal tubules in the cortex. They take back the water and solutes that the tubules reabsorb and return them to the blood.

Nephron / Red blood cells.description: Red blood cells pass single file through the narrow arterioles and capillaries of the kidney. The kidney uses a lot of oxygen for active transport, so this blood supply is vital.

Nephron / Brush border (proximal convolu.description: The brush border is a dense fringe of microvilli on the inner surface of proximal tubule cells. It greatly increases the surface area available for reabsorption.
clinical: Fanconi syndrome
Injury to proximal tubule cells, for example from some drugs or heavy metals, can cause Fanconi syndrome. Glucose, amino acids and phosphate are then lost in the urine.

Nephron / Brush border (proximal straigh.description: The proximal straight tubule also has a brush border of microvilli, which gives it a large absorptive surface. It continues the reabsorption begun in the convoluted part.

Nephron / Connecting tubule.description: The connecting tubule links the distal convoluted tubule to the collecting duct. Its cells respond to aldosterone by reabsorbing sodium and secreting potassium.

Nephron / Cortical collecting duct.description: The cortical collecting duct runs down through the cortex toward the medulla, where aldosterone controls sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion. It also responds to ADH, which makes it more permeable to water.
clinical: Potassium-sparing diuretics
Amiloride blocks sodium channels here and spironolactone blocks aldosterone receptors. Both reduce potassium loss, unlike most other diuretics.

Nephron / Distal convoluted tubule.description: The distal convoluted tubule is a short cuboidal segment after the loop of Henle. It reabsorbs sodium and chloride through the sodium-chloride cotransporter, which is the target of thiazide diuretics.
clinical: Thiazide diuretics
Thiazides such as hydrochlorothiazide block the sodium-chloride cotransporter in this segment. They lower blood pressure and can cause potassium loss.

Nephron / Medullary collecting duct.description: The medullary collecting duct runs down through the medulla to the papilla. It is the final site of urine concentration, where ADH makes it permeable to water.
clinical: Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus
If the collecting duct cannot respond to ADH, large volumes of dilute urine are passed even when ADH levels are high. Lithium and some inherited gene changes cause this.

Nephron / Proximal convoluted tubule.description: The proximal convoluted tubule is the first and longest part of the renal tubule. It reabsorbs most of the filtrate, about two-thirds, including nearly all the glucose and amino acids.
clinical: Acute tubular necrosis
Ischaemia and some nephrotoxic drugs damage these cells most, causing acute kidney injury. Shed cells form the muddy brown casts seen in the urine.
Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors and osmotic diuretics
Acetazolamide blocks bicarbonate reabsorption in this segment, and mannitol, an osmotic diuretic, also acts here.

Nephron / Proximal straight tubule.description: The proximal straight tubule continues from the convoluted part and runs down toward the medulla. It keeps reabsorbing water, salts and nutrients from the filtrate.

Nephron / Thick ascending limb.description: The thick ascending limb is a cuboidal segment that pumps sodium, potassium and chloride out of the filtrate without letting water through. This makes the medulla salty and helps the kidney concentrate urine.
clinical: Loop diuretics
Furosemide and similar drugs block the sodium-potassium-chloride cotransporter here. They are the most powerful diuretics, used for fluid overload and heart failure.

Nephron / Thin ascending limb.description: The thin ascending limb is a simple squamous tube that lets salt leave the filtrate but is impermeable to water. This adds to the salt gradient of the medulla.

Nephron / Thin descending limb.description: The thin descending limb of the loop of Henle is a simple squamous tube that lets water leave the filtrate as it passes down the medulla. The salty surroundings draw the water out.

Nephron / Endothelium (exposed loop).description: The endothelium is the thin, fenestrated lining of the glomerular capillaries. Its gaps let plasma through while holding back blood cells.

Nephron / Glomerular basement membrane (.description: The glomerular basement membrane is a thick mesh of collagen and proteoglycans between the endothelium and the podocytes. It is the main size and charge filter for proteins.
clinical: Basement membrane damage
Changes in the basement membrane, as in diabetic kidney disease, damage the filter and let protein leak into the urine.

Nephron / Glomerular capillary wall.description: The glomerular capillary wall is the filter between the blood and the capsule space. It has three layers: fenestrated endothelium, the glomerular basement membrane and the podocyte foot processes.
clinical: Nephrotic syndrome
Damage to the filter lets large amounts of protein leak into the urine, causing swelling and low albumin in the blood.
Nephritic syndrome
Inflammation of the glomerular capillaries, as in post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, causes blood in the urine, high blood pressure and reduced kidney function.

Nephron / Intraglomerular mesangium.description: Mesangial cells sit between the glomerular capillary loops and support them. They make matrix and can contract, which helps control how much filtration happens.
clinical: IgA nephropathy
Deposits of IgA in the mesangium cause mesangial expansion and proliferation. It is a common cause of recurrent blood in the urine.

Nephron / Parietal layer of Bowman's cap.description: The parietal layer is the outer wall of Bowman's capsule, made of simple squamous epithelium. It is continuous with the proximal tubule at the urinary pole of the glomerulus.
clinical: Crescents
In rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, the parietal cells multiply and form crescents that block filtration.

Nephron / Podocytes on the exposed loop.description: Podocytes are specialized cells that wrap the outside of the glomerular capillaries. Their foot processes interdigitate and leave narrow filtration slits between them.
clinical: Minimal change disease
Flattening and fusion of the podocyte foot processes, called effacement, is the key finding. It causes heavy protein loss and is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children.

Nephron / Visceral layer (podocyte coat).description: The visceral layer is the inner wall of Bowman's capsule, formed by podocytes that cling to the capillaries. It faces the capillary loop and forms the last part of the filter.

clinical: Perinephric abscess
Pus can collect in the fat and fascia around the kidney, often spreading from an infection in the kidney itself. It causes fever and flank pain.

Source section / Arteries.description: This cross-section shows the renal arteries, from the main artery through the segmental, interlobar, arcuate and interlobular branches. Each branch splits into smaller ones on the way out to the cortex.

Source section / Veins.description: This cross-section shows the renal veins, from the small cortical veins through the arcuate and interlobar veins to the large sinus veins that form the renal vein. Renal veins anastomose freely, so a single branch can usually be tied off without causing infarction.

Source section / Nephron wedge.description: This section shows one nephron and its collecting duct within a wedge of kidney tissue. The corpuscle filters the blood, the tubule reabsorbs most of the filtrate, and the duct carries urine down to the papilla.

parts.description: The renal pelvis is the funnel-shaped expansion at the upper end of the ureter, lying inside the renal sinus at the hilum. It gathers urine from the major calyces and narrows at the pelviureteric junction, where it becomes the ureter. It lies behind the renal artery and vein, and in a histology section its lining of transitional epithelium, which can stretch as urine fills it, helps identify it.

The abdominal aorta is the main arterial trunk of the abdomen, continuous with the thoracic aorta through the aortic hiatus (the opening in the diaphragm) at about the level of T12. It lies in front of the vertebral column, slightly left of midline and to the left of the inferior vena cava, and gives off paired renal arteries at about L1 to L2. It ends by dividing into the two common iliac arteries at about the level of L4.

The renal capsule is the thin, tough fibrous membrane that directly surrounds the outer surface of the kidney. It is made of dense irregular connective tissue rich in collagen, with some elastic fibres, and lies just deep to the perirenal fat (the fat packed around the kidney). In a healthy kidney it strips off the cortex easily, and in a histology section it shows as a thin pink band of collagen over the outermost cortex.

parts.description: The renal columns (of Bertin) are extensions of cortex that dip down between neighbouring renal pyramids toward the renal sinus, separating one pyramid from the next. Because they are cortical tissue, they contain renal corpuscles (the filtering units, each a glomerulus and its capsule) and convoluted tubules, unlike the parallel straight tubules that stripe the pyramids. The interlobar arteries and veins run through them from the sinus to the boundary between cortex and medulla, so they are a helpful landmark in a dissection.

The renal papilla is the rounded apex of a renal pyramid, projecting into a minor calyx. Its tip, known as the area cribrosa, is pierced by the openings of the papillary ducts (ducts of Bellini), through which urine drains into the calyx. In a section it is recognised as the narrowed tip of the medulla where the pyramid meets the calyx.

The renal pyramid is a cone-shaped mass of medulla, the inner zone of the kidney, and there are usually 8 to 18 per kidney. Its broad base faces the cortex, while its narrow tip, the papilla, projects into a minor calyx. Its striped appearance comes from parallel straight tubules and collecting ducts, which helps identify it in a section.

Renal sinus fat is the adipose (fatty) tissue that fills the renal sinus, the central cavity of the kidney, packing the spaces around the pelvis, calyces, and renal vessels and nerves. It is continuous through the hilum with the perirenal fat outside the kidney, and it cushions these structures. In a dissection, once the hilum is opened, it appears as yellow fat packed around the pelvis and vessels.

keys: Anterior division of the renal artery
parts.description: The anterior division of the renal artery is one of the two main branches into which the renal artery splits near the renal hilum, the other being the posterior division. It lies in front of the renal pelvis and supplies the front part of the kidney through the apical, upper, middle and lower segmental arteries. Its segmental branches are end arteries, so blockage of one can cause an infarct, an area of tissue death, confined to its segment.

parts.description: Arcuate arteries are the arched branches of the interlobar arteries, running across the bases of the renal pyramids at the corticomedullary junction, the boundary between cortex and medulla. They give rise to the interlobular arteries, which run out through the cortex and give off the afferent arterioles that feed each glomerulus. In a section they appear as small arched vessels lying along the junction between cortex and medulla.

parts.description: Interlobular arteries are small radial branches that arise from the arcuate arteries at the corticomedullary junction (the boundary between cortex and medulla) and run outward through the cortex between adjacent renal lobules. Their key role is to give off the afferent arterioles, the small vessels that carry blood into each glomerulus. In a section they appear as small muscular arteries running radially through the cortex, usually accompanied by interlobular veins.

keys: Posterior division of the renal artery
parts.description: The posterior division of the renal artery is one of the two main branches into which the renal artery splits, the other being the anterior division. It runs behind the renal pelvis as it enters the renal sinus and supplies the back part of the kidney through a single posterior segmental artery. Because it supplies a single segment, a blockage here affects a smaller area than one in the anterior division.

The apical segmental artery is the branch that supplies the apical segment, the top (superior) pole of the kidney. It is one of the four anterior segmental arteries, which usually arise from the anterior division of the renal artery inside the renal sinus. Like all segmental arteries it is an end artery with no connections to its neighbours, so blocking it causes a wedge-shaped infarct (an area of tissue death) confined to the apical segment.

The upper, middle, lower and posterior segmental arteries are four of the five segmental arteries of the kidney, which are branches of the renal artery's anterior and posterior divisions inside the renal sinus. The upper, middle and lower arteries arise from the anterior division and supply the anterior segments, while the posterior artery supplies the back of the kidney. Like all segmental arteries, they are end arteries with no connections to their neighbours, so blocking one causes a wedge-shaped infarct confined to its own segment.

parts.description: Arcuate veins arch over the bases of the pyramids at the corticomedullary junction, the boundary between cortex and medulla, running alongside the arcuate arteries. They collect blood from the interlobular veins and pass it on to the interlobar veins, which carry it toward the renal sinus. In a section they are recognised as veins lying beside the arcuate arteries at this junction.

parts.description: Interlobar veins run beside the interlobar arteries through the renal columns, lying between the pyramids. They collect blood from the arcuate veins at the corticomedullary junction (the boundary between cortex and medulla) and carry it inward toward the renal sinus, where it eventually leaves the kidney in the renal vein. In a dissection they can be recognised as the veins lying alongside the interlobar arteries within each column.

parts.description: Interlobular veins are small veins that run radially through the cortex, accompanying the interlobular arteries between the renal lobules. They collect blood from the stellate veins (small star-shaped venules), which drain the peritubular capillaries (the capillaries wrapped around the tubules), and carry it to the arcuate veins at the corticomedullary junction. In a section they are thin-walled vessels lying beside the interlobular arteries.

keys: Renal vein, common trunk (middle and upper)
parts.description: The common trunk of the middle and upper renal veins is a short vein inside the renal sinus, the central cavity of the kidney that holds its blood vessels, fat and urine-collecting spaces. It forms where the veins draining the middle and upper parts of the kidney join, and it passes this blood on to the renal vein at the hilum, the notch on the inner edge of the kidney. Its branching pattern varies from kidney to kidney, so it may not appear in every dissection.

The lower trunk is a vein inside the renal sinus, the central cavity of the kidney, that drains the region near the lower pole (the rounded lower end of the organ). It carries this blood to the renal vein, either joining the other trunks within the sinus or entering the renal vein directly at the hilum, the kidney's inner notch. Because these venous channels vary between kidneys, their exact arrangement differs from one specimen to the next.

The middle trunk is a vein inside the renal sinus, the kidney's central cavity, that drains the middle part of the kidney, the region lying between the upper and lower parts. Its blood reaches the renal vein either directly at the hilum, the kidney's inner notch, or after joining another trunk within the sinus. Because this branching varies, in some kidneys the middle trunk merges with a neighbouring trunk and cannot be seen as a separate vessel.

The upper trunk is a vein inside the renal sinus, the kidney's central cavity, that drains the upper part of the kidney, the region near the upper pole (the rounded top end of the organ). It may join the middle trunk directly, or through a common channel, before the blood passes to the renal vein at the hilum, the kidney's inner notch. Because these veins vary between kidneys, its size and branching are not fixed.

The endothelium of the afferent arteriole is the single layer of flat cells lining the inside of this small vessel where it enters the glomerulus, the knot of capillaries that filters the blood. It is continuous with the lining of the rest of the arterial system. In a section, look for flattened nuclei that bulge slightly into the lumen, which is the usual way to recognise an endothelial lining.

The smooth muscle of the afferent arteriole is the muscular layer in the wall of the vessel that brings blood into each glomerulus, the knot of capillaries that filters the blood. Its cells contract to narrow the vessel, which lowers pressure in the glomerular capillaries and reduces the glomerular filtration rate, the volume of filtrate formed each minute. It also responds to stretch, keeping filtration steady when blood pressure changes. In a section, look for spindle-shaped cells with elongated nuclei in a thin ring around the lumen.

The endothelium of the efferent arteriole is the single layer of flat cells that lines the inside of the vessel carrying blood away from the glomerulus, the knot of capillaries that filters the blood. It is continuous with the endothelium of the glomerular capillaries, so the lining runs unbroken through the glomerulus. In a section, its flattened nuclei bulge slightly into the lumen, which helps identify it as an endothelial lining.

The smooth muscle of the efferent arteriole is the muscular layer in the wall of the vessel that carries blood away from the glomerulus, the knot of capillaries that filters the blood. When these cells contract, they narrow the outflow and raise pressure inside the glomerular capillaries, which helps keep filtration going when blood flow into the glomerulus falls. In a section, the wall shows spindle-shaped cells with elongated nuclei arranged in a thin ring around the lumen.

The cortical venule is a small, thin-walled vein in the outer part of the kidney, the cortex. It collects blood from the peritubular capillaries, the fine network that wraps around the cortical tubules, and carries it on toward the larger interlobular veins that run through the cortex. In a section, its thin wall and wide lumen help distinguish it from the arterioles beside it.

The deep medullary capillary plexus is a network of thin capillaries in the inner medulla, the deepest part of the renal medulla, which ends at the renal papillae, the tips of the pyramids. It lies among the loops of Henle and collecting ducts, and blood flows through it slowly, which helps maintain the salt gradient of the medulla. In a section, it appears as a fine web of small thin-walled vessels around the tubules near the papilla.

The inner stripe medullary capillary plexus is a network of thin capillaries in the inner stripe of the outer medulla, the band lying between the outer stripe and the inner medulla. Its capillaries are continuous with the descending and ascending vasa recta, the straight vessels that run alongside the loops of Henle and collecting ducts. Because its blood moves slowly, the plexus helps preserve the salt gradient across the medulla.

keys: Red blood cells in ascending vasa rectum 1
Red blood cells in ascending vasa rectum 2
Red blood cells in ascending vasa rectum 3
parts.description: The red blood cells in the ascending vasa recta are erythrocytes travelling back up from the inner medulla toward the cortex. Each cell is small, anucleate (without a nucleus) and biconcave, and in a section it stains pink-red with a paler centre. In these narrow vessels the cells deform as they squeeze through, so they pass without blocking the flow.

keys: Red blood cells in the afferent arteriole
parts.description: Red blood cells in the afferent arteriole are erythrocytes flowing into the glomerulus, the knot of capillaries that filters the blood. Their biconcave discs have no nucleus, so in a section they look like pink-red cells with a paler centre. Their flexible shape lets them squeeze through the narrow arteriole and the glomerular capillaries.

keys: Red blood cells in the cortical venule
parts.description: The red blood cells in the cortical venule are erythrocytes leaving the cortex after they have passed through the capillaries and released their oxygen. In a section they appear as pink-red discs without a nucleus, each with a paler centre where the biconcave shape is thinnest. Because the venule is wider than the capillaries that feed it, several cells can lie side by side across its lumen.

The brush border of the proximal convoluted tubule is the dense fringe of microvilli (tiny finger-like projections) on the luminal, or inner, surface of its cells. These microvilli greatly increase the surface area for reabsorbing glucose, amino acids and salts from the filtrate. In a section, the border is a thick, pink, hair-like edge at the lumen that stains strongly with periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) stain, which marks carbohydrate-rich surfaces.

The brush border of the proximal straight tubule is the fringe of microvilli on the luminal surface of the straight part of the proximal tubule, also called the S3 segment. It is generally shorter and less dense than the brush border of the convoluted part, so the lining looks thinner and less striking. It still absorbs water and salts, and in a section it is recognised by its low cuboidal cells in the outer stripe of the outer medulla.

The connecting tubule is the short segment that joins the distal convoluted tubule to the cortical collecting duct, lying in the cortex, the outer zone of the kidney. Its cells respond to aldosterone, a hormone from the adrenal gland, by reabsorbing sodium through epithelial sodium channels and secreting potassium into the urine. Its wall contains principal cells, which handle sodium and potassium, and intercalated cells, which regulate acid-base balance, the same cell types found in the collecting duct.

The medullary collecting duct is the continuation of the collecting duct through the medulla, running down toward the renal papilla, where the ducts open. Its lower part, in the inner medulla, is the final site where urine is concentrated, because antidiuretic hormone (ADH) makes its cells permeable to water in the salty medulla. In a section it is lined by simple cuboidal to columnar cells and runs among the loops of Henle and vasa recta.

The proximal straight tubule, also called the S3 segment, is the final part of the proximal tubule. It runs down from the cortex into the outer stripe of the outer medulla, reabsorbing water and salts from the filtrate before turning into the thin descending limb of the loop of Henle. Its cells are lower and simpler than those of the convoluted part, with a less prominent brush border.

The glomerular endothelium is the thin, flat lining of the glomerular capillaries, the first layer of the filtration barrier that the blood meets. Its cells are fenestrated, meaning they are pierced by many small pores (fenestrae) that let plasma and small solutes pass while holding back blood cells. Unlike the fenestrae of most other capillaries, these pores have no diaphragm (a thin membrane across the pore), which makes this layer very permeable and the first step in filtration.

Intraglomerular mesangium is the central core of each glomerulus, made of mesangial cells and their matrix, which lies between the glomerular capillary loops. Mesangial cells are contractile and phagocytic, and they secrete the extracellular matrix that supports the loops from within. By contracting or relaxing, they alter the filtering surface area of the capillaries and so help regulate the glomerular filtration rate. In a section, look for nuclei lying in the central stalk between the capillary loops, rather than on their outer surface where the podocytes sit.

The parietal layer of Bowman's capsule is the outer wall of the capsule, a continuous sheet of flattened epithelial cells enclosing the urinary space around each glomerulus. At the urinary pole it becomes cuboidal and continues into the proximal convoluted tubule, and at the vascular pole it turns over as the visceral layer. In a section it is a thin, pale lining of flat cells, set apart from the capillary tuft by the urinary space. Proliferation of its cells forms the crescents seen in crescentic glomerulonephritis.

parts.description: Podocytes are specialised epithelial cells of the visceral layer of Bowman's capsule, wrapping around the outside of the glomerular capillaries. Each has a large cell body bulging into the urinary space, and primary processes that branch into interdigitating foot processes (pedicels) resting on the basement membrane. The narrow gaps between neighbouring foot processes, the filtration slits, are bridged by a slit diaphragm, a thin membrane that acts as a size-selective barrier to proteins. In a section, look for large nuclei lying outside the capillary loops in the urinary space.

The podocyte coat is the visceral layer of Bowman's capsule, the inner wall of the capsule formed by podocytes that wrap around the outside of each glomerular capillary. Its cells lie on the glomerular basement membrane, and their interdigitating foot processes, separated by filtration slits, form the final barrier through which plasma is filtered. In a section, the visceral layer is the cell layer hugging the capillary loops, separated from the parietal layer by the urinary space.

The renal fascia, also called Gerota's fascia, is a sheath of extraperitoneal connective tissue that encloses the kidney, its perirenal fat and the suprarenal gland. Its anterior and posterior layers fuse above the gland and at the lateral edge, but stay open below, where the ureter passes. It anchors the kidney to the posterior abdominal wall, and outside it lies the pararenal fat. Clinically, it tends to confine perirenal haemorrhage and abscess.

Perirenal fat, also called the adipose capsule, is the fat lying between the fibrous capsule of the kidney and the renal fascia, thickest around the borders and poles. It cushions the kidney and helps hold it in place, and it runs through the hilum to join the fat of the renal sinus. Loss of this fat, as in rapid weight loss, can let the kidney drop (nephroptosis) and kink the ureter. On CT it shows as dark fat, and inflammation can make it streaky, a finding called perirenal stranding.

The fibrous (renal) capsule is a thin, tough layer of dense connective tissue that hugs the outer surface of the cortex. It is made mainly of collagen, with some elastic fibres, and in a healthy kidney it strips off easily. At the hilum it turns inwards to line the renal sinus and blends with the adventitia of the calyces and vessels. Because it barely stretches, acute swelling in pyelonephritis or obstruction causes severe loin pain.

The renal cortex is the outer, granular, reddish-brown zone of the kidney, lying between the capsule and the bases of the pyramids, roughly 1 cm thick. It contains all the renal corpuscles and the convoluted tubules, which give it a granular look, and it receives about 90 per cent of renal blood flow. In a section, the cortex is recognised by its glomeruli, seen as small round bodies, and by the medullary rays that run into it from the pyramids. Thinning on ultrasound signals chronic kidney disease.

The renal columns, also called the columns of Bertin, are extensions of cortical tissue that dip down between neighbouring pyramids towards the renal sinus. The interlobar arteries and veins run through them, so they are a useful landmark for locating those vessels in a section. An unusually large column can look like a mass on ultrasound, a pseudotumour known as column of Bertin hypertrophy.

Medullary rays, also called pyramids of Ferrein, are pale, radial striations that run from the base of each pyramid out into the cortex. Each ray is a bundle of straight tubules, mainly collecting ducts and the straight parts of the proximal and distal tubules, so the medulla visibly continues into the cortex along them. A ray with the cortical labyrinth around it forms a renal lobule, which is bounded by interlobular arteries and drained by a collecting duct system.

The renal pyramids are the cone-shaped masses of the renal medulla, of which there are usually 8 to 18 in each kidney. Each base faces the cortex at the corticomedullary junction, marked by the arcuate vessels, and each apex, the papilla, projects into a minor calyx. They look darker and striped because they are packed with parallel nephron loops, collecting ducts and vasa recta, creating an osmotic gradient from about 300 mOsm/kg at the base to about 1200 mOsm/kg at the papilla, which lets antidiuretic hormone (ADH) concentrate urine.

The renal papillae are the rounded tips of the pyramids, projecting into the minor calyces. Each is pierced by 10 to 25 openings of the papillary (Bellini) ducts, the area cribrosa, through which urine drips into the calyx. The papilla has the most concentrated interstitium, the tissue fluid between the tubules, and a relatively poor blood supply in the kidney, so it is vulnerable to necrosis in analgesic (NSAID) abuse, diabetes, sickle cell disease and severe pyelonephritis.

Medullary striations are the streaks that make the medulla look striped, running from base to papilla. They are straight collecting ducts, thick and thin limbs of the loops of Henle and bundles of vasa recta, all running parallel within the medulla. In a section, look for these parallel tubules in the medulla rather than the coiled tubules of the cortex. In medullary sponge kidney, the collecting ducts dilate into small cysts, and stones often form in them.

The minor calyces are 7 to 14 cup-shaped tubes, each lined by urothelium, that fit over the tip of one papilla or a compound papilla at a pole. They collect urine from the papillary ducts, and their smooth muscle acts as a pacemaker that starts peristalsis towards the ureter. In a section, look for a urothelium-lined cup wrapping round a papilla, with sinus fat outside its wall. In acute obstruction the fornices, the weakest parts of the calyces, can tear and leak urine into the renal sinus.

The major calyces are two or three wider tubes (superior, middle and inferior), each formed by the union of two or three minor calyces, and they open into the renal pelvis. In a section, look for the wider channels in the sinus between the minor calyces and the pelvis. A staghorn calculus, a branching stone, fills the pelvis and extends into the calyces like antlers.

The renal pelvis is the funnel-shaped upper end of the ureter, lying in the renal sinus and collecting urine from the major calyces. Its wall is urothelium over smooth muscle and adventitia, and it narrows at the pelviureteric junction, where it passes into the ureter, the first of the ureter's three narrowings. A stone that lodges at this junction is a common cause of renal colic.

The ureter is a muscular tube about 25 to 30 cm long and 3 to 4 mm wide, running on the psoas muscle from the renal pelvis to the bladder. Its wall has urothelium on a lamina propria that folds into a star-shaped lumen, with inner longitudinal and outer circular smooth muscle in the upper two-thirds. Urine is moved by peristaltic waves, not gravity. In a section, its star-shaped lumen within a thick muscular wall identifies it; a stone lodged in it causes colic.

Renal sinus fat is the fat packed into the renal sinus, the central space of the kidney that opens at the hilum. It surrounds the renal pelvis, the calyces and the branches of the renal vessels, nerves and lymphatics, and it is continuous with the perirenal fat. In a fresh section it is yellow and lobulated, filling the gaps between the pelvis, vessels and nerves. A renal cell carcinoma that invades it is staged T3a.

The hilum is the vertical slit on the concave medial border of the kidney, at about the level of L1, through which the renal vessels, nerves, lymphatics and ureter enter and leave the renal sinus. From anterior to posterior the structures are the renal vein, the renal artery and the renal pelvis, which may be remembered as VAP (vein, artery, pelvis). The left hilum sits a little higher than the right because the liver pushes the right kidney down.

The renal artery is the main artery supplying each kidney, arising from the side of the abdominal aorta at about L1 to L2, just below the superior mesenteric artery. It runs behind the renal vein and in front of the renal pelvis to reach the hilum, where it divides into anterior and posterior divisions. Its segmental branches are functional end arteries, so blockage of one causes a wedge-shaped infarct. In a section, its thick muscular wall and its position between the vein and pelvis identify it.

The segmental arteries are the branches of the renal artery that run in the renal sinus, usually five in number (apical, upper, middle, lower and posterior), each supplying one of the renal segments. Each segment depends on its own artery, which has little collateral supply, so blockage of one can infarct that segment alone. In a section, look for them in the sinus fat, between the renal pelvis and the renal vein.

The interlobar arteries are branches of the segmental arteries that run between the renal pyramids, within the renal columns, out towards the corticomedullary junction. At that junction each gives off arcuate arteries, which arch over the pyramid bases and feed the interlobular arteries. In a section, look for them in the renal columns between adjacent pyramids, accompanied by the interlobar veins.

The arcuate arteries are arching vessels that run along the corticomedullary junction, where the cortex meets the bases of the pyramids. They are continuations of the interlobar arteries, and they give off the interlobular (cortical radiate) arteries that climb into the cortex. In a section, look for a vessel arching across the pyramid bases just beneath the cortex.

The cortical radiate (interlobular) arteries are the small arteries that run outwards from the arcuate arteries through the cortex, between the renal lobules. Along their length they give off afferent arterioles, which carry blood to the glomeruli. In a section, they appear as small radial vessels in the cortex, running towards the capsule between adjacent medullary rays.

The renal vein is the main vein of each kidney, leaving the hilum and carrying blood to the inferior vena cava. It lies in front of the renal artery and pelvis, and on the left side it passes between the aorta and the superior mesenteric artery. In a section, the renal vein is the most anterior and widest of the hilar vessels, and it receives the segmental veins from the sinus.

The segmental veins, also called sinus veins, lie in the renal sinus and drain the kidney's segments, joining to form the renal vein. They run alongside the segmental arteries, usually lying in front of them, and carry blood out of the sinus through the hilum. Their walls collapse easily, so in a section they often look like flattened, empty channels in the sinus fat.

The interlobar veins run through the renal columns beside the interlobar arteries, between adjacent pyramids. They collect blood from the arcuate veins at the corticomedullary junction and carry it towards the renal sinus, where they join the sinus veins. In a section, they are the thin-walled, wide-lumened companions of the interlobar arteries.

The arcuate veins run along the corticomedullary junction, arching over the bases of the pyramids. They collect blood from the interlobular veins of the cortex and pass it into the interlobar veins, which carry it towards the sinus. In a section, look for a vein arching across the pyramid bases just beneath the cortex, lying alongside the arcuate artery.

The cortical radiate (interlobular) veins run outwards through the cortex from the arcuate veins towards the capsule, between the renal lobules. They collect blood from the stellate veins just beneath the capsule and from the peritubular capillaries, and deliver it to the arcuate veins. In a section, look for thin-walled radial veins running between adjacent medullary rays, alongside the cortical radiate arteries.

The nephron tubule is the long epithelial tube running from Bowman's capsule to the collecting duct, made of the proximal convoluted tubule, the loop of Henle and the distal convoluted tubule. Its segments reabsorb about 99 per cent of the filtrate and secrete wastes and drugs into the urine. In a section, the proximal tubule is recognised by its cuboidal cells with a dense brush border, while the distal tubule has similar cells without one.

The collecting duct is the final tubule that collects urine from many nephrons, receiving it through the connecting tubules and carrying it down through the medulla to the papilla. In the cortex it runs in the medullary rays, and in the medulla it is lined by pale principal cells, with scattered darker intercalated cells. Principal cells respond to antidiuretic hormone (ADH) by inserting aquaporin-2 water channels, which allow water to be reabsorbed and urine to be concentrated.

The renal corpuscle is the filtering unit of the nephron, made of a glomerulus (a tuft of fenestrated capillaries) enclosed in Bowman's capsule. Blood enters at the vascular pole through the afferent arteriole and leaves through the efferent arteriole, while filtrate leaves at the urinary pole. Plasma is filtered across three layers: the fenestrated endothelium, the glomerular basement membrane and the slit diaphragms between podocyte foot processes. In a section, look for a round body in the cortex with a capillary tuft inside a clear urinary space.

A nephron is the functional unit of the kidney, and each kidney contains about a million of them. Each nephron runs from a renal corpuscle through the proximal tubule, loop of Henle and distal tubule to a connecting tubule that drains into a collecting duct. Its corpuscle lies in the cortical labyrinth, the granular outer cortex, and its loop dips into the medulla, most deeply in the juxtamedullary nephrons whose corpuscles sit at the cortex-medulla border.
